Treat it as untrusted, and do not fetch or submit data to it automatically
Follow it only if it uses HTTPS
Follow it if the domain looks familiar
questions.exp: A link that arrived inside retrieved content is untrusted, so do not fetch it or submit anything to it automatically. Auto-following turns your agent into a channel an attacker controls: the destination decides what comes back, and a request carrying parameters can exfiltrate whatever is in scope. HTTPS authenticates the server and encrypts transport; it says nothing about whether the destination is trustworthy, which is the confusion worth clearing up here. A familiar-looking domain is weaker still, since lookalike domains are the entire point of that technique. Show it to the user and let them decide.
why: Auto-following lets content the attacker controls choose your agent's next request, and any parameters go with it.
Correct. Treat it as untrusted - do not fetch it or send data to it without a person deciding.
HTTPS authenticates the server and encrypts transport. It says nothing about whether the destination should be trusted.
Lookalike domains exist precisely to appear familiar, which makes visual similarity the weakest possible check.

questions.q: The purpose of validating model output before acting on it is:
opts: To improve response quality
Because generated values are untrusted input to whatever consumes them next
To reduce token cost
It is unnecessary with structured outputs
questions.exp: Model output is untrusted input to whatever consumes it next. A generated identifier that reaches a query, a path that reaches a filesystem call, a URL that reaches a fetch - each is a value from outside your trust boundary, and the ordinary rules for untrusted input apply. That framing puts the check in the right place: validate at the boundary where the value is used, not wherever it happened to be produced. Structured outputs guarantee shape rather than meaning, so a schema-valid value can still be wrong or hostile, and validation remains necessary alongside it.
why: Validation rejects bad values rather than improving generation. Quality is a separate concern from safety at the boundary.
Correct. Generated values are untrusted input to whatever consumes them, so the ordinary rules for untrusted input apply.
Validation runs in your code and consumes no tokens. Cost is unrelated to whether you check the output.
Structured outputs guarantee shape, not meaning. A schema-valid identifier can still be wrong or hostile.

questions.q: An MCP server you depend on ships a new version that renames a tool. Your agent breaks. The durable fix is:
opts: Hardcode the old tool name in the prompt
Pin the server version and treat tool contracts as a versioned dependency, upgrading deliberately
Ask the model to guess the new name
Retry until it works
questions.exp: Treat tool contracts as a versioned dependency: pin the server version, and upgrade deliberately after checking what changed. That is the same discipline you would apply to any library whose API your code calls, for the same reason - an unpinned dependency can change the interface underneath a working system at a time you did not choose. Hardcoding the old name in the prompt describes a tool that no longer exists. Asking the model to guess turns a deterministic contract into a probabilistic one, and retrying repeats a call that will keep failing for the same reason.
why: Naming a tool that no longer exists does not make it exist. The contract changed, not the wording.
Correct. Pin the version and treat tool contracts as a versioned dependency, upgrading deliberately after reviewing what changed.
Guessing turns a deterministic contract into a probabilistic one, which is the opposite of what a dependency should be.
The call fails for a stable reason. Retrying repeats it without changing anything.

questions.q: The main problem MCP is designed to solve is:
opts: Making models reason better
The N-by-M integration problem — every client needing bespoke connectors for every data source
Reducing token cost
Replacing HTTP
questions.exp: MCP addresses the N-by-M problem: without a standard, every client needs a bespoke connector for every data source, so the integration count multiplies rather than adds. A shared protocol turns that into N plus M - write a server once and any MCP-aware client can use it. That is the whole argument, and it is an ecosystem argument rather than a capability one. The model is unchanged, tokens are unchanged, and HTTP is still the transport underneath. Being precise about this matters because MCP gets loosely used to mean any kind of tool integration.
why: Reasoning is a property of the model. A connection protocol does not change how well it thinks.
Correct. The N-by-M integration problem - a shared protocol turns per-client-per-source connectors into write-once servers.
Cost is driven by tokens. A protocol for connecting tools does not change what a request costs.
MCP runs over existing transports including HTTP. It standardises tool and data access rather than replacing the web.

questions.q: An MCP resource differs from an MCP tool in that a resource:
opts: Executes an action with side effects
Exposes data for the model to read, rather than an action to perform
Is always faster
Requires no schema
questions.exp: A resource exposes data for the model to read; a tool performs an action. The distinction is about side effects, and honouring it makes a server predictable: reads that look like actions invite unnecessary approval prompts, and actions exposed as inert data hide the fact that something changes when they run. That second case is the dangerous one. Speed is an implementation property rather than a protocol distinction, and resources are described too - a client needs to know what it is reading - so it is not a matter of one having a schema and the other not.
why: That describes a tool. The read-versus-act distinction is precisely what separates the two primitives.
Correct. A resource exposes data to read, where a tool performs an action - the distinction is side effects.
Speed depends on the implementation. A resource backed by a slow query is slower than a fast tool.
Resources are described too. A client needs to know what it is reading, so both carry definitions.

questions.q: Before connecting a third-party MCP server to an agent with write access, the most important step is:
opts: Check that it is popular
Review what tools it exposes and what permissions they require, and scope access accordingly
Confirm it is open source
Confirm it is fast
questions.exp: Review what the server exposes and what permissions those tools require, then grant the narrowest access that works. Connecting a third-party server with write access hands an external party the ability to define actions your agent can take, so the tool list and its permission requirements are the security surface. Tool descriptions themselves arrive from the server, which makes them untrusted content too. Popularity, licence and speed are all reasonable selection criteria, and none of them tells you what the server can do once connected.
why: Popularity indicates adoption rather than safety, and a widely used server can still request more access than your agent should grant.
Correct. Review the exposed tools and their required permissions, then scope access to the narrowest that works.
Open source allows inspection but does not perform it. The audit is the value, and it still has to be done.
Latency is a performance property. It says nothing about what the server is able to do with write access.

questions.q: An MCP prompt primitive is best described as:
opts: A system prompt the server forces on the client
A reusable, parameterized template the server offers for common tasks
The user's typed message
A cached response
questions.exp: An MCP prompt is a reusable, parameterised template the server offers - a way to package a common task so clients do not each reinvent the wording. It is offered rather than imposed: the client decides whether to use it, which keeps control with the application. That framing also makes the trust boundary clear, since a template arriving from a server is content from outside your system and deserves the same scepticism as any other server-supplied text. It is neither the user's message nor a cache of past responses.
why: The server offers templates; it does not impose a system prompt. The client decides whether to use one.
Correct. A reusable, parameterised template the server offers for common tasks, which the client may choose to use.
The user's message is conversational input. A prompt primitive is a template the server publishes.
Caching stores prior results. A prompt primitive is a template for constructing new requests.

questions.q: A benefit of standardizing tool access through MCP rather than hardcoding integrations is:
opts: Tools become free to run
Servers can be developed, versioned, and reused independently of any one client
The model no longer needs tool descriptions
Authentication becomes unnecessary
questions.exp: Standardisation lets servers be built, versioned and reused independently of any single client, which turns integrations into shared infrastructure instead of per-application work. A server written once serves every MCP-aware client, and it can evolve on its own release cycle - which is also why pinning versions matters. What does not change is everything below the protocol: tools still cost whatever they cost to run, the model still needs good descriptions to choose well, and authentication is still required and arguably more important once a third party is involved.
why: Execution cost is unchanged by how a tool is reached. A protocol does not make the work behind it free.
Correct. Servers can be developed, versioned and reused independently of any one client, which makes integrations shared infrastructure.
Descriptions are how the model decides what to call. MCP standardises delivery rather than removing the need for them.
Authentication is still required, and matters more once a third-party server is in the path.

questions.q: Your agent connects to an MCP server that suddenly returns a tool description telling the model to exfiltrate credentials. The correct design assumption is:
opts: Server-supplied descriptions are trusted configuration
Tool descriptions from a server are untrusted content and must not be able to escalate the agent’s permissions
The model will always recognize and ignore this
This cannot happen over MCP
questions.exp: Tool descriptions arriving from a server are untrusted content. They are text from outside your system that reaches the model's context, which makes them an injection vector, so the design assumption has to be that they may be hostile and must not be able to escalate what the agent is permitted to do. The defence is the same as for any injection: bound the permissions rather than rely on recognition. Treating server-supplied descriptions as trusted configuration is the mistake, and expecting the model to always notice is the assumption these attacks exist to defeat.
why: Configuration you control is trusted. Text arriving from a third-party server at run time is not, even though it functions as configuration.
Correct. Server-supplied descriptions are untrusted content and must not be able to escalate the agent's permissions.
Relying on the model to notice is the assumption injection attacks are built to defeat. Bound the permissions instead.
Nothing in the protocol prevents a server sending whatever description it chooses. This is exactly the threat to design against.

questions.q: Your service targets Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5. A request sends `thinking: {type: 'enabled', budget_tokens: 4096}`. What happens?
opts: HTTP 400 — budget_tokens was removed on these models; adaptive thinking replaced it
It works, but the budget is silently capped at max_tokens
It is ignored and the request runs with thinking disabled
It works on Sonnet 5 but returns 400 on Opus 5
why: Correct. The parameter was removed on this generation, so validation fails before any tokens are spent. Switch to adaptive thinking and set output_config.effort.
The API does not silently rewrite parameter values. An unsupported parameter is rejected, not clamped — silent capping would hide the migration entirely.
There is no silent-ignore path, and it would be worse than the 400: you would pay for a request that quietly did not do the thing you asked for.
Both are the same generation here. The split runs between 4.6 and 4.7, not between the Sonnet and Opus families.
questions.exp: A fixed thinking budget is not merely discouraged on Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and 4.7 — the parameter was removed, so the request fails validation with a 400 before any tokens are spent. The replacement is `thinking: {type: 'adaptive'}`, which lets Claude decide how much to think per request, with depth steered by `output_config.effort` (low through max) rather than a token count. `budget_tokens` still works on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 as a deprecated escape hatch, and is still required on pre-4.6 models — so the same code can be valid on one model and a hard error on the next. Check the parameter shape per generation, not once.

questions.q: In a multi-turn conversation with Extended Thinking enabled, how should the application format the assistant's previous turn in the `messages` array?
opts: Include both the `thinking` block (with its signature) and the `text` content block unaltered
Delete the `thinking` block and keep only the `text` block to save tokens
Convert the `thinking` block into a `user` role message
Re-encrypt the signature using a local private key
why: Correct. Both blocks unchanged, signature included, since the signature is what verifies the block was not altered.
Dropping thinking blocks to save tokens can trigger ordering and signature errors rather than degrading quietly.
Thinking is assistant-side reasoning. Recasting it as a user message misrepresents the turn structure entirely.
The signature is verified by the API, not by you. Re-encrypting it locally guarantees rejection.
questions.exp: Pass previous thinking blocks back unchanged, signature included, alongside the text block. The signature is what lets the API verify the block was not altered, so editing or reconstructing it breaks the turn, and dropping thinking blocks to save tokens can trigger ordering and signature errors rather than quietly working. The rule is unchanged rather than untouched: reading or displaying a summarised block is fine, modifying it is not. On current models the raw chain of thought is never returned, so what you echo back may carry an empty thinking field.

questions.q: You are building a computer-use agent with `computer_20251124`. How should you size screenshots?
opts: 1080p as the default, dropping to 720p or 1366x768 when cost matters more than fidelity
The highest resolution the display supports, always
The smallest readable size, since resolution does not affect accuracy
It makes no difference — screenshots are billed at a flat rate
why: Correct. 1080p is the balanced default, with lower resolutions available when cost outweighs fidelity.
Maximum resolution costs the most per step and rarely improves accuracy on a legible interface — an expensive default in a per-step loop.
Resolution does affect accuracy: below a point the model can no longer resolve the control it needs to click.
Screenshots are images and images are billed by the tokens they resolve to, which scales with resolution.
questions.exp: Screenshot resolution is the main cost and accuracy lever in a computer-use loop, and it is a genuine trade rather than a maximise-one-side choice. 1080p balances the two well; 720p or 1366x768 cut cost meaningfully where the interface is still legible at that size. Current models read screenshots at much higher resolution than earlier ones, and coordinates map directly to image pixels, so no scale-factor arithmetic is needed on the way back — but that fidelity is billed, and an agent taking a screenshot per step pays it on every iteration. Measure on your own interface rather than assuming.

questions.q: Which JSON-RPC 2.0 message method is sent by an MCP client to discover available server-side read-only data assets?
opts: resources/list
tools/list
prompts/list
roots/list
why: Correct. resources/list discovers read-only data assets, matching the resource primitive.
tools/list returns invocable actions with side effects rather than data to read.
prompts/list returns reusable templates, a third primitive distinct from both data and actions.
roots/list concerns the workspace boundaries the client exposes to the server, not assets the server offers.
questions.exp: The list methods map one-to-one onto the primitives, so choosing between them is really a question of which primitive you want. Resources are data the model can read, which makes resources/list the discovery call for read-only assets; tools/list returns invocable actions and prompts/list returns templates. roots/list is different in kind: it concerns the filesystem or workspace boundaries the client exposes to the server rather than assets the server offers. Keeping the primitives distinct is what makes the protocol predictable to implement against.

questions.q: What is the role of `isError: true` in an MCP `tools/call` response payload?
opts: It informs the model that the tool execution failed (e.g. file not found), allowing the model to handle the error gracefully
It terminates the MCP connection immediately
It triggers an HTTP 500 internal server error on the host
It deletes the tool from the server
why: Correct. It tells the model the execution failed, so the failure becomes something it can reason about and adapt to.
The connection stays open. This is a normal protocol response that happens to carry a failure result.
It is a field within a successful response rather than a transport-level error on the host.
Nothing is removed. The tool remains available and can be called again.
questions.exp: isError reports that the tool execution failed, and it reports it to the model, which is the point. The failure becomes information the model can reason about and adapt to rather than an exception that terminates the run. That distinction matters for agent design: a tool error the model can see leads to a retry or a different approach, whereas a dropped connection leads to an abandoned run and a silent empty result leads to a confidently wrong conclusion. It is a normal, successful protocol response that happens to carry a failure result.

questions.q: A developer is sending a native PDF document to the Messages API. Which content block structure is valid?
opts: `{ type: 'document', source: { type: 'base64', media_type: 'application/pdf', data: pdfBase64 } }`
`{ type: 'file', path: 'C:/docs/report.pdf' }`
`{ type: 'pdf_raw', binary: buffer }`
`{ type: 'text', text: '<pdf>' + rawBytes + '</pdf>' }`
why: Correct. A document block with a base64 source and the application/pdf media type, sent in the request body.
The API cannot reach your filesystem. A local path is meaningless to a service running elsewhere.
There is no such block type, and raw binary is not a valid content payload.
Splicing raw bytes into a text block corrupts them. PDFs need the document block type rather than text.
questions.exp: PDFs go in as a document content block with a base64 source and the application/pdf media type, placed before the text block that asks about them. Everything travels in the request body, which is the general principle worth carrying: the API has no access to your filesystem, so a local path means nothing to it. Two limits are worth remembering - the base64 string must have no newlines, and there are request-size and page ceilings. For documents reused across calls, upload once via the Files API and reference the file id instead of re-sending the bytes each time.

questions.q: How many cache breakpoints (`cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}`) can be defined in a single Anthropic Messages API request?
opts: Up to 4 cache breakpoints
Exactly 1 cache breakpoint
Unlimited cache breakpoints
Up to 100 cache breakpoints
why: Correct. Four per request, which is enough to mark several stability tiers independently.
One would force a single boundary, which is too coarse when tools, system prompt and history change at different rates.
There is a hard limit. Unlimited breakpoints would make the cache key space unmanageable.
The limit is far lower than this, and a prompt needing dozens of boundaries has a structural problem.
questions.exp: Up to four breakpoints per request. The limit matters when you have several stability tiers - tools, then a fixed system prompt, then a document set, then conversation history - because each breakpoint marks a point that can be reused independently. Four is usually plenty; if you find yourself wanting more, the prompt structure is probably the thing to simplify. Two related limits are worth holding alongside it: the minimum cacheable prefix varies by model and is not ordered by recency, and a breakpoint looks back at most twenty content blocks to find a prior entry.

questions.q: Prompt caching minimums differ by model. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Every model shares a single 1,024-token minimum
They vary by model and are not ordered by recency — the newest models cache from 512 tokens while Haiku 4.5 needs 4,096
The minimum scales with the model's context window
There is no minimum; any prefix can be cached
why: A single shared minimum would be easier to remember and is not what the API does — the figures differ by model.
Correct. Per-model and not ordered by recency, which is why the figure has to be checked rather than inferred.
Context window and cache minimum are independent. Haiku 4.5 has the smallest window and one of the highest minimums.
There is a minimum, and falling below it fails silently rather than erroring — the most expensive way for a limit to work.
questions.exp: The minimum cacheable prefix is per-model and deliberately unintuitive: Opus 5 caches from 512 tokens, Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 from 1,024, and Opus 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 from 4,096 — so a newer model is not automatically the more permissive one. This matters because a prefix below the threshold fails silently: no error, just cache_creation_input_tokens of zero and full price on every request. A 3,000-token system prompt caches on Opus 5 and does not on Haiku 4.5. Verify with the usage fields rather than assuming, and re-check the figure whenever you change model.

questions.q: When defining a custom tool in `tools: [...]`, what happens if the developer sets `tool_choice: {type: 'any'}`?
opts: The model is forced to call at least one of the provided tools rather than generating plain text
The model selects any random model tier
The model chooses whether to execute bash or python
The API throws an invalid parameter exception
why: Correct. The model must call one of the supplied tools rather than producing plain text.
Model selection is set by the model parameter. tool_choice governs tool behaviour within a request.
It does not enumerate specific tools. any means one of the tools you supplied, whichever the model judges best.
It is a valid parameter and a documented mode rather than an error condition.
questions.exp: tool_choice of any forces the model to call one of the provided tools rather than replying with plain text. It is useful when a tool call is the only sensible outcome - a routing step, or an extraction that must land in a schema - and it removes the possibility of a conversational answer where you expected structured action. Use it deliberately, because forcing a call when none applies pushes the model to pick the least-bad tool rather than saying it cannot help. Note it is a valid parameter, and some platforms have additional constraints on combining it with other settings.

questions.q: A long-running request using a server-side tool returns `stop_reason: 'pause_turn'`. Your loop should:
opts: Treat it as a failure and restart the task
Re-send the conversation including the assistant turn, so the server resumes where it left off
Append a user message saying 'Continue.' and send again
Increase max_tokens and retry the original request
questions.exp: A server-side tool loop has its own iteration limit, and reaching it produces `pause_turn` - work in progress rather than a failure. Re-sending the conversation with the assistant turn appended lets the server pick up from where it paused. Adding a 'Continue.' message is the intuitive move and the wrong one: the API detects the trailing server-tool block and resumes on its own, so the extra turn is noise in the transcript. Worth knowing that SDK tool runners do not auto-resume this, so a paused turn can end a run silently unless your loop checks for it.
why: It is not a failure. Restarting discards work the server has already done and will hit the same limit again.
Correct. Re-send with the assistant turn appended and the server resumes from where it paused.
The API detects the trailing server-tool block and resumes automatically, so an extra instruction just adds noise.
The output ceiling was not the constraint. This is a server-side tool iteration limit, not a token limit.

questions.q: When an API request receives HTTP 429 Rate Limit, which response header should be parsed to determine the exact sleep duration?
opts: `anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-reset` or `retry-after`
`x-server-uptime`
`content-length`
`set-cookie`
why: Correct. retry-after or the rate-limit reset headers give the exact wait, turning backoff from a guess into a measurement.
Server uptime is diagnostic metadata unrelated to your quota or when it resets.
Content length describes the response body size and says nothing about rate limits.
Cookies are session metadata. They carry no rate-limit information.
questions.exp: Parse retry-after, or the rate-limit reset headers, to learn exactly how long to wait. That turns backoff from a guess into a measurement: you sleep until the window actually replenishes rather than doubling blindly and either hammering too early or idling too long. The headers also report your limit and what remains, which lets a client pace itself before it hits 429 at all. The other headers listed are ordinary HTTP metadata with no relationship to throttling - reaching for them is a sign of guessing rather than reading the documented contract.

questions.q: Why is 'Full Jitter' combined with Exponential Backoff when retrying failed API requests?
opts: It randomizes retry intervals to prevent synchronized thundering herd spikes on the API gateway
It encrypts the payload with random bytes
It increases the token generation speed on subsequent retries
It forces the request to switch to a different cloud region
why: Correct. Randomised intervals prevent synchronised retry waves, which is how a brief overload becomes a sustained one.
Jitter varies timing rather than payload content. Nothing about the request is encrypted differently.
Retry timing has no effect on generation speed. The model performs identically whenever the request arrives.
Jitter affects when a retry is sent, not where. Routing is unrelated.
questions.exp: Jitter randomises the retry interval so clients that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same moment. Without it, exponential backoff synchronises a fleet: everyone waits one second, then two, then four, and each wave arrives together - which is how a brief overload becomes a sustained one. Full jitter picks uniformly from zero to the current backoff window, spreading the load across the interval. It is a coordination fix rather than anything to do with encryption, speed or routing, and it matters most exactly when the most clients are failing.

questions.q: In the Messages API, where must the `system` prompt be placed?
opts: In the top-level `system` parameter of the request object
As a message with `role: 'system'` inside the `messages` array
Appended to the end of the user prompt inside `<system>` tags
In the HTTP request headers
why: Correct. A top-level system parameter on the request object, separate from the messages array.
That is the convention in some other APIs and a common porting mistake. The top-level field is the standard mechanism here.
Tags in the user prompt make it ordinary user content rather than a system instruction with its own standing.
Headers carry authentication and beta flags. Prompt content belongs in the request body.
questions.exp: The system prompt is a top-level parameter on the request, alongside model, max_tokens and messages - not a message inside the array. That is a common porting mistake from APIs that use a system role in the conversation, and it matters for caching too: system renders after tools and before messages, so its position in the prefix determines what can be cached. Note that some current models additionally support system-role messages inside the array for mid-conversation instructions, which is a different mechanism from the top-level field and does not replace it.

questions.q: When implementing semantic search over a 50,000-page document store, what is the standard role of embeddings vs Claude?
opts: Vector embeddings retrieve top-K relevant chunks; Claude synthesizes and reasons over the retrieved context
Embeddings generate the final user answer; Claude only counts tokens
Embeddings are used only for image classification
Claude converts the entire 50,000-page database into a single binary file
why: Correct. Embeddings retrieve the likely-relevant chunks; the model reasons over what comes back and produces the answer.
Embeddings produce vectors for similarity search. They cannot generate an answer, and token counting is unrelated.
Embeddings apply to text as readily as images. Restricting them to classification misdescribes the technique.
No conversion of that kind happens. The corpus stays where it is and relevant portions are retrieved per query.
questions.exp: The division of labour is retrieval versus reasoning. Embeddings turn text into vectors so similarity search can find the passages likely to be relevant, and the model then reads those passages and reasons over them to produce an answer. Neither half substitutes for the other: embeddings cannot synthesise or explain, and sending fifty thousand pages to the model is neither affordable nor effective. The quality ceiling is usually set by retrieval rather than by the model - if the right passage is not retrieved, no amount of reasoning capability recovers it, which is why retrieval evaluation matters.

questions.q: You need to know whether a large prompt will fit and what it will cost, before sending it. The right approach is:
opts: Estimate with a general-purpose tokenizer library such as tiktoken
Call the token-counting endpoint with the same model you will use
Divide the character count by four
Send it and read the usage figures from the response
questions.exp: Token counts are model-specific, so the only accurate answer comes from the counting endpoint called with the model you actually intend to use. The common shortcuts are all biased in the same direction: tiktoken is OpenAI's tokenizer and undercounts Claude tokens substantially, more so on code and non-English text, and a characters-over-four heuristic is rougher still. Sending the request and reading usage afterwards does tell you the truth, but only once you have already paid for it - which defeats the purpose when the question is whether to send it at all.
why: That is a different provider's tokenizer. It undercounts Claude tokens noticeably, and the gap widens on code and non-English input.
Correct. Token counts are model-specific, so count with the model you will actually use.
A character heuristic is rougher than a foreign tokenizer and varies wildly by content type.
This is accurate but arrives after you have already been billed, which is too late if the question is whether to send it.

questions.q: What happens when you set `temperature: 0.0` on Claude Sonnet 5?
opts: The request is rejected — non-default sampling values are not accepted
The model uses greedy decoding, giving identical output every run
It is silently ignored and the request proceeds normally
It halves output token cost by shortening responses
why: Correct. Non-default sampling values are rejected on Sonnet 5, so this is a validation failure rather than a behaviour change.
Greedy decoding was never the guarantee even where temperature was accepted — low temperature narrows sampling without making output reproducible.
The API does not silently drop unsupported parameters. Silent-ignore would be worse: your code would look correct while doing nothing.
Temperature never affected pricing. Cost follows the tokens generated, not how they were sampled.
questions.exp: Sampling parameters were removed on this generation. Opus 5, Opus 4.8 and 4.7 reject temperature, top_p and top_k outright, and Sonnet 5 rejects any non-default value — so an integration carrying temperature=0 forward from an older model fails validation rather than behaving deterministically. Steer behaviour with prompting and structured outputs instead. Worth knowing even on models that still accept it: temperature=0 never guaranteed identical output across runs. It narrowed sampling, which is not the same as determinism, so any pipeline that depended on byte-identical responses was already resting on an assumption the API did not make.

questions.q: A developer wants to guarantee that Claude returns JSON adhering strictly to a JSON Schema for tool calls. Which property should be configured?
opts: Define `input_schema` with required properties and standard JSON schema types in the tool definition
Add 'Please try your best' in the description
Set `temperature: 1.0`
Send the prompt through a Base64 filter
why: Correct. Explicit types and required properties in the input_schema define the contract, with strict mode available to enforce it.
Encouragement in a description is not a constraint. The model may still produce something that does not fit.
Sampling parameters do not govern output structure, and current models reject them outright.
Encoding changes representation rather than structure. It does nothing to enforce a schema.
questions.exp: A well-defined input_schema with explicit types and a required list is the foundation - it tells the model exactly what shape the arguments must take. For an actual guarantee rather than strong guidance, add strict: true on the tool definition, which requires additionalProperties: false and enforces conformance. Note the boundary: this guarantees structure, not meaning. A date range with the end before the start satisfies any reasonable schema and is still impossible, so semantic validation belongs in your tool implementation regardless of how tight the schema is.

questions.q: Why is Extended Thinking particularly valuable for complex competitive programming and mathematical proofs?
opts: It allows Claude to verify logic, test edge cases, and backtrack before writing code tokens
It automatically compiles the code on an external GPU
It translates Python into Assembly language
It disables all safety filters
why: Correct. It lets the model verify logic, test edge cases and backtrack before committing to output tokens.
No code is executed. The reasoning happens in the model rather than on external hardware.
No translation occurs. Reasoning is about working through the problem, not converting between languages.
Reasoning depth and safety behaviour are unrelated. Nothing about thinking changes what the model will decline.
questions.exp: Reasoning before generating lets the model work through the problem, test cases against it, and abandon an approach that does not hold - all before committing to output tokens. That is exactly what competitive programming and proofs need, because the cost of a wrong first move is high and backtracking mid-answer is expensive. On current models this is adaptive thinking with an effort level rather than a fixed budget: Claude decides how much reasoning each problem warrants. The trade-off is real, so sweep effort on your own problems rather than assuming the highest setting is always best.

questions.q: When streaming responses using `client.messages.stream(...)`, what is the primary benefit to end-user experience?
opts: Significantly reduced perceived latency (Time-to-First-Token) as tokens appear in real time
50% discount on total token pricing
Automatic recovery from network disconnections without client code
Higher maximum output token limit
why: Correct. Tokens appear as they are generated, so the user sees progress rather than a blank wait.
There is no pricing difference. Streaming changes delivery rather than what the tokens cost.
Reconnection is your client's responsibility. Streaming does not add automatic recovery.
The output ceiling is set by the model and your parameter. Streaming does not raise it, though it makes large outputs practical.
questions.exp: Streaming reduces perceived latency by rendering tokens as they are generated, so the user sees progress instead of a blank pause. It does not make generation faster - total completion time is essentially unchanged - which is worth being precise about, since the fix is to the experience rather than the throughput. It is also the practical requirement for large outputs: non-streaming requests with a high ceiling risk client timeouts, which is why streaming is recommended above roughly 16K max_tokens regardless of any user-experience consideration.

questions.q: What is the Batches API turnaround SLA for processing batch workloads?
opts: Results are returned within 24 hours with a 50% discount on input and output tokens
Results are returned in exactly 5 seconds
Results take 30 days to process
Results are only processed on weekends
why: Correct. Within 24 hours at a 50% discount on input and output tokens, which is why latency-tolerant work belongs there.
Batch processing is explicitly asynchronous. Anything needing a response in seconds should use the standard endpoint.
The commitment is 24 hours, and most batches finish well within it.
Processing is continuous rather than scheduled. There is no weekly window.
questions.exp: Batches process asynchronously and return within 24 hours, at half the token price on both input and output. In practice most complete far sooner, but 24 hours is the commitment to design against - so the fit is work with no user waiting: nightly pipelines, bulk classification, backfills. The discount is the reason to route eligible work there deliberately rather than running everything synchronously. Results also arrive in arbitrary order, so key them by your own custom identifier rather than by position, which is the mistake that produces mismatched records.

questions.q: In an MCP server implementation, what method is called when the client requests to execute a parameterized prompt template?
opts: prompts/get
prompts/list
tools/call
resources/subscribe
why: Correct. prompts/get retrieves and fills a specific template, where list only enumerates what is available.
prompts/list enumerates available templates. It is the discovery half rather than the invocation.
tools/call invokes an action with side effects, which is a different primitive from a prompt template.
resources/subscribe registers interest in changes to a resource and is unrelated to prompt templates.
questions.exp: prompts/get retrieves and fills a specific template, where prompts/list enumerates what is available. The pattern holds across the protocol: each primitive has a list method for discovery and a corresponding call for use, which is what makes it predictable to implement against. tools/call invokes an action and resources/subscribe registers interest in changes to a resource - different primitives entirely. Keeping the discovery and invocation halves distinct in your own server design is what lets clients explore capabilities without triggering side effects.

questions.q: When returning a `tool_result` to Claude, how must the message role and structure be formatted?
opts: `role: 'user'` with content array containing `{ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: '...', content: '...' }`
`role: 'tool'` with plain text string
`role: 'system'` with JSON object
`role: 'assistant'` with error code
why: Correct. A user-role message whose content array holds tool_result blocks, each referencing its tool_use_id.
There is no tool role in this API, and the result needs the structured block rather than a plain string.
The system prompt sets behaviour. Tool output belongs in the message history in its own block type.
The assistant role is the model's own turns. Your application's results are supplied as user content.
questions.exp: Tool results go back as a user-role message whose content array holds tool_result blocks, each carrying the tool_use_id it answers. The user role is the part that surprises people - it is the channel for anything your application supplies back to the model, and there is no separate tool role in this API. Return every result for a turn in a single user message: splitting parallel tool results across several messages trains the model away from making parallel calls. Failures go back the same way with is_error set, rather than being dropped.

questions.q: With adaptive thinking enabled, what does `max_tokens` limit?
opts: Thinking tokens and response text together
Only the visible response text
Only the thinking blocks
The total conversation context, including your input
why: Correct. One ceiling covers both, which is why thinking-on-by-default can truncate a workload whose max_tokens was tuned without it.
If it capped only the response, thinking would be unbounded and spend unpredictable. The point of the ceiling is that it bounds total generation.
The reverse of the real behaviour. Capping thinking alone would leave the answer unbounded, and would not explain the truncated answers people actually see.
That is the context window, a separate limit with its own stop reason: model_context_window_exceeded. max_tokens governs only what this turn generates.
questions.exp: `max_tokens` is a single ceiling over everything the model generates on that turn — reasoning and answer share it. This is the most common surprise when moving a workload onto a model where thinking is on by default: a limit sized tightly around the expected answer now truncates mid-sentence, and you see `stop_reason: max_tokens`. The fix is to raise `max_tokens` or lower `output_config.effort` so less of the budget goes to reasoning. It is not a context limit — exhausting the context window is a different stop reason, `model_context_window_exceeded`.

questions.q: Why does modifying a variable at the very start of a prompt invalidate all downstream prompt cache blocks?
opts: Prompt Caching is an exact prefix-matching tree; any early token delta invalidates all subsequent cache keys
The server restarts whenever a prompt changes
Prompt cache blocks only last for 1 millisecond
Cache blocks are tied to the client IP address
why: Correct. It is an exact prefix match, so any early change alters every downstream cache key at once.
Nothing restarts. This is a property of how cache keys are computed rather than of server lifecycle.
Entries live for minutes or an hour depending on the TTL you choose, not milliseconds.
Caches are scoped to content and model rather than to a network address.
questions.exp: Caching matches on an exact prefix, so the cache key for any point depends on every token before it. Change something early and every downstream key changes with it, which invalidates all of them at once. That is why ordering by stability is the whole discipline: unchanging content first, volatile content after the last breakpoint. The failure is silent, which is what makes it expensive - there is no error, just a cache read of zero and full price on every call. Watch the cache-read usage field to confirm it is actually working.

questions.q: When chunking code files for RAG, why is AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) chunking superior to fixed-character chunking?
opts: It splits code cleanly along function and class boundaries, preserving complete syntactic and semantic units
It encrypts the code to prevent plagiarism
It reduces code size by 90%
It converts JavaScript into Rust
why: Correct. Splitting on function and class boundaries keeps each chunk a complete, self-contained syntactic unit.
Chunking is a segmentation strategy for retrieval. It has no relationship to encryption or access control.
Chunking divides content rather than compressing it. Total size is essentially unchanged.
No language translation occurs. Chunking decides where to split, not what the code is.
questions.exp: AST chunking splits along function and class boundaries, so each chunk is a complete syntactic unit that makes sense on its own. Fixed-character chunking cuts wherever the counter runs out, which routinely splits a function from its signature or a class from its methods - and a retrieved fragment missing its declaration is close to useless for answering a question about it. The general principle extends beyond code: chunk on the structure the content already has rather than on a character count, which is why heading-aware chunking works better for documents.

questions.q: What is the maximum context window on current Claude Opus and Sonnet models?
opts: 200,000 tokens
4,096 tokens
8,192 tokens
1,000,000 tokens
why: That is Haiku 4.5's window and was the previous generation's norm. It no longer describes current Opus and Sonnet models.
This is far below any current model and describes a much older generation entirely.
That figure is closer to an output ceiling on older models than to any current context window.
Correct. 1M tokens on current Opus and Sonnet models, with Haiku 4.5 the 200K exception.
questions.exp: Current Opus and Sonnet models offer a 1M-token context window. Haiku 4.5 is the exception at 200K, which is worth remembering because the 200K figure was the norm for an earlier generation and is still widely repeated as if it applied to everything. A large window changes what is architecturally possible - whole codebases and document sets in a single request - but it does not make doing so wise: cost scales with what you send, and relevant material still competes with everything else present. Retrieval remains the better default for narrow questions over large corpora.

questions.q: In an agentic loop, what condition must terminate the autonomous tool-calling cycle?
opts: The model returns `stop_reason: 'end_turn'` (or hits a maximum iteration safety ceiling)
The user closes their browser tab
The computer battery reaches 50%
The hard drive runs a defragmentation check
why: Correct. end_turn signals natural completion, with your own iteration or spend ceiling as the safety bound.
Client-side events do not govern a server-side loop, and a run may continue regardless of what a browser does.
Hardware state is unrelated to the agent's control flow.
Disk maintenance has no relationship to whether a model has finished requesting tools.
questions.exp: The loop ends when the model stops asking for tools - stop_reason of end_turn - or when your own safety ceiling on iterations or spend is reached. Both halves matter: the first is the natural completion, and the second is what stops an ambiguous task looping indefinitely at unbounded cost. The ceiling should also define what happens when it is hit, because a loop that simply stops leaves the work in an undefined state, whereas one that hands off with its partial results is recoverable. The termination condition is a property of your harness, not of the environment around it.

questions.q: What transport protocol should be selected when building an MCP server intended to run as a local CLI sub-process?
opts: Standard Input/Output (stdio)
Server-Sent Events (SSE) over HTTPS
Bluetooth Low Energy
FTP
why: Correct. stdio suits a local subprocess - no port, no listener, and nothing else can reach it.
HTTP-based transport suits remote servers. For a local subprocess it adds a network surface you do not need.
Bluetooth is not an MCP transport and is unsuited to local process communication.
FTP is a file transfer protocol and is not used for JSON-RPC messaging.
questions.exp: For a server running as a local subprocess, stdio is the natural transport: the parent process spawns the server and they exchange JSON-RPC messages over standard input and output, with no network listener, no port and no authentication surface. That last point is the real benefit - a local server that never opens a socket cannot be reached by anything other than its parent. HTTP-based transports are the right choice for remote servers, where the network is the point. The other options are not transports the protocol uses at all.

questions.q: What is the recommended client behavior when an API call fails with HTTP 529 (Overloaded)?
opts: Apply exponential backoff with jitter and retry up to 3-5 times before falling back
Immediately crash the application and alert the CEO
Spam 50 simultaneous retry requests
Delete the API key and create a new account
why: Correct. Exponential backoff with jitter for a bounded number of attempts, then fall back rather than retrying indefinitely.
This turns a transient, retryable condition into a user-visible outage.
Parallel retries add load to a system that just reported being overloaded, extending the condition.
The key is not the problem, and rotating credentials to evade capacity limits addresses nothing.
questions.exp: A 529 means the service is temporarily overloaded, which is a retryable condition. Back off exponentially with jitter for a bounded number of attempts, then fall back - to a different model, a queue, or a degraded response - rather than retrying forever. Jitter is what stops every client retrying in the same instant and extending the overload. The SDKs implement this by default, so much of it is handled if you are not hand-rolling HTTP. Crashing turns a transient condition into an outage, and parallel retries add load to a system already reporting too much.

questions.q: When structuring complex inputs with multiple files in a prompt, which formatting standard provides optimal clarity for Claude?
opts: Wrap each file in `<file name='filepath'>content</file>` XML tags with clear document index headers
Paste all files together as one continuous paragraph with no spaces
Convert all files into emoji icons
Upload only the file size in bytes
why: Correct. Tagged, path-labelled files give clear boundaries and let the model cite which file an answer came from.
Concatenating without structure removes every boundary, so the model cannot tell where one file ends and the next begins.
Substituting icons for content discards the content itself, which is what the model needs to read.
File size carries none of the content. There would be nothing for the model to work with.
questions.exp: Wrapping each file in tags with its path gives the model an unambiguous boundary and a name to refer to, so it can cite which file a claim came from and you can trace the answer back. An index header helps further on large sets by giving an overview before the contents. This is the same delimiting principle that matters for security: clearly bounded, labelled content is far less likely to be read as instruction than an undifferentiated wall of text, which is one of the ways prompt injection gets a foothold.

cards.b: model, max_tokens and a messages array are required; system, tools and output_config are optional. max_tokens being mandatory surprises people coming from APIs that default it — and it caps thinking and response text together, so a limit sized around the answer will truncate once thinking is on. Sampling parameters are not optional but rejected on current models.

end_turn (finished naturally) · max_tokens (truncated) · tool_use (run a tool and return the result) · stop_sequence · refusal (terminal) · pause_turn (server-tool loop paused; re-send to resume) · model_context_window_exceeded. Branch on this before reading content: truncated, refused and finished all arrive as a successful response with content in it.

Claude returns a tool_use block, your code executes the tool, you append a tool_result carrying the matching tool_use_id, and the loop repeats until it stops requesting tools. Two common errors: treating tool_use as a failure, and returning an empty result instead of an error — which makes the model conclude the data does not exist rather than that the call failed.

Reuses a processed prefix across calls at roughly a tenth of the input rate. It is a prefix match, which governs everything else: stable content first, volatile content after the last breakpoint, or the cache silently never hits. The failure is invisible — no error, just a cache read of zero and full price on every call. Watch the cache-read usage field.

Asynchronous bulk processing at half price on input and output, returned within 24 hours. Ideal where nobody is waiting: nightly pipelines, bulk classification, backfills. Two operational details — most batches finish well inside the window but design against 24 hours, and results arrive in arbitrary order, so key them by your own identifier rather than position.

Server-sent events delivering tokens as they are generated. It does not make generation faster; it removes the wait before anything appears, which is what users experience as slowness. It is also the practical requirement above roughly 16K max_tokens, where non-streaming requests risk client timeouts regardless of any user-experience consideration.

Untrusted content — web pages, emails, documents, third-party tool descriptions — carrying text that tries to hijack the model. The model is not malfunctioning; it processed text it was given. Delimiting helps and is not sufficient. What bounds the damage is least-privilege tooling and approval gates, because those hold whether or not anyone noticed the attack.

An open standard letting clients discover and call tools, resources and prompts exposed by servers. The argument is combinatorial: without it, every client needs a bespoke connector for every source, so integrations multiply rather than add. Write a server once and any compatible client can use it — an ecosystem gain rather than a capability one.

Tools (actions the model invokes) · Resources (data it reads) · Prompts (reusable templates the server offers). The dividing line is side effects, and honouring it keeps a server predictable: an action exposed as inert data hides the fact that something changes when it runs. If unsure which a capability is, ask whether calling it twice differs from calling it once.

Workflow = fixed predefined steps: predictable, cheap, easy to test and debug. Agent = a model-directed loop with tools: open-ended and far less predictable. The criterion for wanting a loop is narrow — the number and order of steps cannot be known in advance. Reaching for one because a task feels sophisticated is how teams pay loop cost for a pipeline.

The project instruction file Claude Code loads on every session — conventions, build and test commands, architecture notes, constraints not obvious from any single file. Keep it to things that stay true, since stale guidance there is worse than none. It is checked in, so credentials must never go in it and changes go through review like any other.

Server-side only, from environment variables or a secret manager, never in client code or a repository. Anything in front-end code is readable by any visitor regardless of bundling. The server tier is also the only place you can enforce per-user rate limits, authorisation and logging — so this is where the controls live, not merely where the secret hides.

Documents first inside clear delimiters, instruction at the end. The instruction sits closest to where generation begins, which measurably improves instruction-following on long inputs, and the delimiters tell the model where source material ends — without that boundary, text inside a document can read as a command you did not issue.

cards.f: How is thinking depth controlled on current Claude models?
cards.b: With thinking set to adaptive, so Claude decides how much to think per request, and output_config.effort (low through max) steering the depth. Note effort is nested inside output_config rather than top-level. The old fixed budget_tokens dial is rejected with a 400 on Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and 4.7 — code carrying it forward fails validation rather than degrading.

cards.f: How must thinking blocks be handled in multi-turn conversation history?
cards.b: Pass them back unchanged, signature included, alongside the text block. The signature is what verifies the block was not altered, so editing or reconstructing it breaks the turn — and dropping them to save tokens can trigger ordering and signature errors rather than quietly working. Reading a summarised block is fine; modifying it is not.

cards.f: What beta header is required for Anthropic Computer Use tools?
cards.b: anthropic-beta: computer-use-2025-11-24, paired with the computer_20251124 tool version. Beta headers and tool version strings are dated and move together, so a header carried forward from an older integration will not match the current tool. Check both against the current documentation whenever you revisit a computer-use integration.

cards.f: What are the 3 built-in Computer Use tools?
cards.b: computer_20251124 (screen, mouse, keyboard), bash_20250124 (shell), text_editor_20250728 (file editing). All three are client-side: your harness owns the environment and executes every action, which is exactly where an approval gate belongs for anything irreversible. Note the text editor's type and name change together — mismatching them returns a 400.

cards.f: How are native PDF files passed to the Messages API?
cards.b: As a document content block with a base64 source and the application/pdf media type, placed before the text block that asks about it. Everything travels in the request body — the API cannot reach your filesystem, so a local path means nothing. For documents reused across calls, upload once via the Files API and reference the file id instead.

cards.f: What are the two standard MCP transport layers?
cards.b: stdio for a local subprocess, and an HTTP-based transport for remote servers. stdio is the right default for anything local: no port, no listener, no authentication surface, and nothing but the parent process can reach it. HTTP transport is for when the network is the point, and it brings the access-control questions that go with it.

cards.f: What is the purpose of roots/list in MCP?
cards.b: It lets the client tell the server which workspace directories it may inspect. Read the direction carefully: this is a boundary the client declares inward, not a privilege the server holds — the name misleads people into reading it as superuser access, which inverts a security control. In multi-tenant environments it is what keeps one tenant's server away from another's files.

It lets an MCP server request a model completion from the host client, with user consent. The consent step is the point: it keeps control of model usage and cost with the application rather than the server, and it means a third-party server cannot silently spend your tokens or route your data through a prompt you never saw.

cards.f: What causes a Prompt Cache invalidation?
cards.b: Any change to tokens before the breakpoint, because caching is an exact prefix match — one altered byte changes every downstream cache key at once. The usual culprits are a timestamp, a session id or a per-user greeting placed early. It fails silently, which is what makes it expensive: no error, just a cache read of zero and full price.

cards.f: What is the maximum number of requests allowed in a single Batches API file?
cards.b: Up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch, whichever is reached first, with results returned within 24 hours. Most batches complete well inside that window, but 24 hours is what you design against. Results come back in arbitrary order, so key them by your own custom identifier rather than by position in the file.

cards.f: Which response header specifies the exact timestamp when token rate limits reset?
cards.b: anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-reset, an ISO 8601 timestamp. Parsing it turns backoff from a guess into a measurement — you wait until the window actually replenishes rather than doubling blindly. The related headers report your limit and what remains, which lets a client pace itself before it hits 429 at all rather than discovering the limit by tripping it.

A server-side tool loop reached its iteration limit — work in progress rather than a failure. Re-send the conversation including the assistant turn and the server resumes where it paused. Do not append a 'Continue.' message: the API detects the trailing server-tool block itself. SDK tool runners do not auto-resume this, so a paused turn can silently end a run.

lessons.b:
This cert assumes you can write basic code and are comfortable with concepts like variables, functions, and JSON — but it does not assume you've used an LLM API before. This lesson fills that gap.

What you're actually building

When you 'use the Claude API,' you're writing code that sends an HTTP request containing text (and instructions) to Anthropic's servers, and gets back a response containing more text. That's the whole shape of it — everything else in this cert (tools, agents, MCP, streaming) is refinement on top of that basic request/response exchange.

Terms this cert assumes you know, defined quickly

  • REST API: a way for programs to talk to a server over HTTP using standard verbs (mostly POST here) and structured data — you'll send JSON, you'll get JSON back
  • JSON: the text format ({"key": "value"}) almost everything in this cert is expressed in — requests, responses, tool schemas, all of it
  • SDK: a language-specific software package (Anthropic publishes ones for Python, TypeScript, and others) that wraps the raw HTTP calls in convenient functions, so you're rarely constructing requests by hand
  • Token: the unit Claude reads and writes in (~¾ of a word on average) and the unit you're billed by — max_tokens caps how long a response can be
  • Latency: how long a request takes to get a response — matters a lot for interactive features, less for background batch jobs

If any of REST, JSON, or environment variables are genuinely new to you, it's worth spending 20 minutes with a general web-development primer before diving into the API Mechanics lesson — this cert moves fast on the assumption those are already comfortable.

Everything is one endpoint

It helps to hold a single mental model: tools, structured outputs, thinking, caching and streaming are all features of the same Messages request, not separate APIs to learn individually. A request carries a model, an output ceiling, and a list of messages; everything else is an optional field that changes what comes back. Most of what looks like a large surface area is really a handful of parameters combined.

Three properties that explain most surprises

  • The API is stateless. There is no session, no server-side history. Continuing a conversation means resending it, which is why cost grows with conversation length and why caching matters so much in practice.
  • `max_tokens` bounds everything generated, reasoning included. A limit sized around the expected answer will truncate once thinking is on.
  • `stop_reason` is the first thing to read. Truncated, refused, finished and paused all return a successful response with content in it. Only the stop reason distinguishes them, and code that skips the check will hand a user half an answer that looks whole.

What has changed recently, and why it matters

Several patterns you will find in older tutorials now fail outright rather than degrading. Sampling parameters are rejected on current models. A fixed thinking budget is rejected; adaptive thinking with an effort level replaced it. Prefilling the assistant turn to force JSON is rejected; structured outputs replaced it. Recognising these is worth real marks and real debugging time, because the failure is a validation error rather than a subtle behaviour change.

Key takeaways
  • The API is just HTTP request in, HTTP response out — everything else builds on that.
  • You'll work mostly through an SDK, not raw HTTP, but understanding the underlying shape matters for debugging.
  • Comfort with JSON and basic REST concepts is assumed going forward.

🛠️ Developer Foundations: SDK Lifecycle & Architecture

The Anthropic developer ecosystem centers around official SDKs for Python (anthropic) and TypeScript (@anthropic-ai/sdk). All SDKs support automatic retries with exponential backoff and jitter, typed streaming helpers, and first-class tool calling primitives.

// TypeScript Developer Initialization Pattern
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';

const anthropic = new Anthropic({
  apiKey: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
  maxRetries: 3, // Built-in jittered exponential backoff
  timeout: 30 * 1000, // 30s timeout
});

The Messages API is the foundation everything else sits on. Three things are required on every request: model, max_tokens, and a messages array. system and tools are optional. Sampling parameters such as temperature are rejected on current Claude models — behaviour is steered through prompting and structured outputs instead.

One call, one response — the API itself holds no memory of past calls.

The API is stateless

There is no server-side conversation store and no session identifier. To continue a conversation you resend the full prior history — user and assistant turns — on every call. This is why prompt caching matters so much in practice: the repeated prefix grows with the conversation.

Always read stop_reason before the content

The terminal reason tells you why generation ended, and each value needs different handling:

  • end_turn — natural completion. The answer is whole.
  • max_tokens — truncated because it hit the cap you set. Raise the cap or continue the response; do not present it as finished.
  • tool_use — expected control flow, not an error. Run the tool and return a tool_result.
  • stop_sequence — hit a stop string you supplied.
  • refusal — generation stopped on safety grounds. Terminal: surface it rather than retrying the identical request.
  • pause_turn — a long-running server-side tool loop paused; re-send to resume.

Consuming content without checking stop_reason is how truncated and refused output reaches users looking like a complete answer.

Streaming

Streaming delivers tokens incrementally over server-sent events. It does not make generation faster — it makes it feel faster by removing the wait before anything appears, which is why it is the standard fix for a chat UI that feels sluggish to start. Lowering max_tokens to make responses arrive sooner just truncates them.

Rate limits and retries

An HTTP 429 is normal operation at volume, not an outage. The robust client retries with exponential backoff and respects the rate-limit headers. Failing on the first 429 makes ordinary throttling look like a failure; rotating keys to evade limits is a terms problem rather than an engineering fix; and fanning the same request out in parallel amplifies the pressure that caused it.

Handling a response correctly
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=history,          # full prior turns, every call
)

if resp.stop_reason == "refusal":
    handle_refusal(resp)       # terminal - do not retry blindly
elif resp.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
    continue_response(resp)    # truncated, not finished
elif resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    run_tools_then_reply(resp) # expected control flow
else:
    deliver(resp)              # end_turn
Key takeaways
  • model, max_tokens, and messages are required; system and tools are optional.
  • Sampling parameters are rejected on current models — steer with prompting.
  • The API is stateless: resend the full history each turn.
  • Branch on stop_reason before consuming content.
  • refusal and pause_turn are stop reasons worth handling explicitly.
  • Streaming improves perceived latency; 429 means back off, not fail.
Common pitfalls

Assuming server-side memory. There is no session id that carries state for you.

Treating tool_use as an error. It is the model asking you to run something.

Retrying a refusal unchanged. It will generally refuse again; the request needs to change or be escalated.

Production Python SDK Code — Retries with Exponential Backoff & Jitter

When calling the Messages API at scale, handling HTTP 429 rate limit responses requires exponential backoff with full jitter to avoid thundering-herd retry spikes:

import time, random
from anthropic import Anthropic, RateLimitError, APIError

client = Anthropic()

def call_with_backoff(prompt, max_retries=5):
    base_delay = 1.0
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            return client.messages.create(
                model="claude-sonnet-5",
                max_tokens=1024,
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
            )
        except RateLimitError as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
            sleep_time = (base_delay * (2 ** attempt)) + random.uniform(0, 1)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)
        except APIError as e:
            if e.status_code >= 500 and attempt < max_retries - 1:
                time.sleep((base_delay * (2 ** attempt)) + random.uniform(0, 1))
            else:
                raise

Context is 1M tokens, except where it isn't

Current Opus and Sonnet models offer a 1M-token context window; Haiku 4.5 is the exception at 200K. The 200K figure was the norm for an earlier generation and still gets repeated as if it applied everywhere, which is worth catching in review. A large window changes what fits in a single request — whole codebases, large document sets — but it does not change whether sending all of it is a good idea: cost scales with what you send, and material still competes with everything else present for attention.

Files and images travel in the request body, not as attachments

The API has no filesystem access, so a local path means nothing to it — an image or a PDF has to be encoded into the request itself, as a content block with a base64 source and the correct media type, placed before the text that asks about it. For a document you reuse across many calls, encoding it every time is wasteful; the Files API lets you upload once and reference the resulting file id instead of resending the bytes each call. Two limits worth remembering on the base64 path: the encoded string must contain no newlines, and there are request-size and page ceilings to design around.

429 and 529 are different problems, same medicine

A 429 means you personally have exceeded a rate limit; a 529 means Anthropic's service is temporarily overloaded and has nothing to do with your quota. Both are retryable, and both call for exponential backoff with full jitter for a bounded number of attempts — jitter matters most exactly here, since a 529 by definition means many clients are contending for capacity at once, and un-jittered retries from all of them arrive together and prolong the overload they are trying to wait out. After the attempt budget is exhausted, fall back — a queue, a degraded response, a different model — rather than retrying forever.

Two mechanisms make model output safe to consume programmatically: structured outputs, which constrain generation to a JSON schema, and tool use, which lets the model request actions your code performs. Both replace the fragile pattern of asking for JSON in prose and repairing whatever comes back.

The tool-use loop — steps 2 through 5 can repeat multiple times before end_turn.

Structured outputs

Supplying a schema through output_config.format constrains decoding so the response conforms by construction — no parse failures, no retries for malformed JSON. For tools, strict: true gives the same guarantee for generated arguments.

An important limit: schemas guarantee shape, not meaning. A response can be perfectly schema-valid and still contain an end date before its start date. Semantic validation remains your job.

Writing a tool the model will use correctly

The description is the interface the model reasons over, so detail there is the single strongest lever on tool-calling accuracy. Say what the tool does, when to call it, when not to, and what each parameter means — a description stating its trigger condition outperforms one stating only its function. Tight schemas do the complementary half, narrowing what can be produced.

Adding more tools works against both. Every definition costs context on every request, and near-miss options multiply as the surface grows, so a large tool list degrades exactly the decision it was meant to enable.

The loop, and the two ways it goes wrong

A `tool_use` stop reason is expected control flow: run the tool, append a `tool_result` carrying the matching `tool_use_id`, call again. Two mistakes are common enough to name. Treating it as an error produces an agent that appears to abandon every task needing a tool. And returning an empty result instead of an error makes the model conclude the data does not exist rather than that the call failed — a confidently wrong answer instead of a visible failure.

When the model requests several tools at once, return every result in a single user message. Splitting them across messages teaches the model its parallel calls were handled sequentially, and it batches less in future turns.

Structural guarantees and their limit

`strict: true` on a tool definition guarantees inputs conform to the declared schema — it sits on the tool, not on `tool_choice`, and needs `additionalProperties: false` with an explicit `required` list. What it cannot do is validate meaning. A date range with the end before the start satisfies any reasonable schema and is still impossible, so semantic checks stay in your tool implementation and return an actionable error the model can correct on the next turn.

Forcing a call, and when not to

`tool_choice` of `any` compels the model to call one of the supplied tools rather than replying in prose, which is useful when a tool call is the only sensible outcome. Use it deliberately: forcing a call when none applies pushes the model to select the least-bad tool instead of saying it cannot help.

Outdated technique

Older guides teach prefilling — seeding the assistant turn with { so generation continues as JSON. Current Claude models reject a prefilled final assistant turn with a 400 error. Use structured outputs instead.

The tool-use loop

Tool use is a conversation, not a single call. The model returns a tool_use block; your application executes the tool and sends the outcome back as a tool_result in the same message history; generation continues with that result available. Starting a fresh conversation with the result discards the reasoning that led to the call.

Tool descriptions are prompts

What most improves tool-calling accuracy is not the number of tools but the quality of their descriptions and schemas. State when a tool should be used and when it should not, and constrain arguments in the schema. Registering many overlapping tools creates opportunities to confuse similar options; terse one-word names strip out the information needed to choose.

Errors belong in the loop

When a tool fails, return the error to the model as a tool_result so it can retry or adapt. Crashing the loop throws away everything completed so far; silently returning empty results is worse, because the model then reasons confidently from nothing.

Schema first
output_config = {
  "format": {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name":  {"type": "string"},
        "email": {"type": "string"}
      },
      "required": ["name", "email"],
      "additionalProperties": false
    }
  }
}

The contract is declared before generation and enforced during it — then validated downstream anyway, because shape is not meaning.

Key takeaways
  • Structured outputs (output_config.format) guarantee schema-conformant JSON.
  • strict: true gives the same guarantee for tool arguments.
  • Schemas constrain shape, never semantics — keep validating.
  • Assistant-turn prefilling errors on current models; do not use it.
  • Return tool outcomes as tool_result in the same conversation.
  • Tool descriptions and schemas, not tool count, drive selection accuracy.
Common pitfalls

Regex-repairing prose JSON. The failure mode structured outputs exists to remove.

Swallowing tool errors. Silent empty results produce confidently wrong answers.

Widening a schema to stop failures. That increases the range of bad input rather than fixing it.

Complete Multi-Turn Tool Execution Loop (Python SDK)

def run_agent_tool_loop(user_query):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_query}]
    tools = [{
        "name": "get_stock_price",
        "description": "Fetch current stock price for a ticker.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"ticker": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["ticker"]
        }
    }]
    
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools,
        messages=messages
    )
    
    if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
        # Extract requested tool call
        tool_block = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
        result = execute_real_tool(tool_block.name, tool_block.input)
        
        # Append assistant turn and tool_result user turn
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        messages.append({
            "role": "user",
            "content": [{
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": tool_block.id,
                "content": str(result)
            }]
        })
        # Second call delivers final answer with tool result in context
        return client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=messages)
